item.title: Hybrid Humility: The Long Walk Toward Ourselves
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Hybrid Humility: The Long Walk Toward Ourselves

One question that can help us move beyond outsourced power.

Posted August 8, 2026

Key points
  • Intellectual humility sharpens judgment and counteracts the bias ego brings.
  • AI tools can inflate self-perception, especially among those who feel tech-savvy.
  • Tools are aids, not substitutes, for authentic self-development.
Hybrid humility starts from the inside out. It invites us to ask who we are (not).
Source: Walther/ChatGTP/2026

A reporter cornered Marie Curie in 1904 and asked whether radium might cure disease. She refused to guess. Nothing had been demonstrated, she said, and she would not pretend otherwise. Her caution vanished the moment marketers got hold of her discovery. Drugstores sold radium water by crate. Chocolate came laced with it. A Pittsburgh steel heir named Eben Byers drank roughly 1,400 bottles of a radium tonic called Radithor, convinced he had found a private engine of vitality. His jaw dissolved. His skull grew holes. The Wall Street Journal summed up the era in 10 words: "The Radium Water Worked Fine Until His Jaw Came Off."

Every Century Gets Its Glow

Byers believed he had acquired a superpower. So did the physicists who promised, mid-century, that atomic energy would soon be too cheap to bother metering. So did the scientists who announced in 2000 that they had sequenced the "book of life," a phrase so seductive that Bill Clinton and Tony Blair read it aloud together on television. Twenty years on, the metaphor needed far more footnotes than anyone expected, and the promised wave of personalized cures arrived as a trickle rather than a flood. Then came the internet, sold as a leveler of hierarchies and a connector of continents. Then smartphones, an oracle in every pocket. Each episode felt like arrival. Looking back, each one reads as a rung, useful and real, on a ladder nobody had finished building.

We are standing on the newest rung now. Ask yourself, honestly: Does typing a question into a chat window and receiving a fluent paragraph feel any less magical than radium felt in 1904?

The Mirror We Keep Building

Here, the pattern gets interesting rather than merely repetitive. Researchers at Aalto University recently tested how people judge their own performance after using a chatbot to solve reasoning problems. Ordinarily, skill and self-assessment move together: People who know the least tend to overrate themselves, and people who know the most tend to hedge. Psychologists call this the Dunning-Kruger effect. The Aalto team found it flipped entirely once AI entered the picture. Everyone overestimated their performance, and the users who considered themselves most AI-literate overestimated it hardest. The tool got sharper. Our read on our own sharpness got worse.

A glowing bottle of radium water and a glowing chat interface play the identical trick on the mind: Both invite a person to mistake borrowed capability for personal capability.

Humility Is Not Surrender

Studies on intellectual humility, the meta-cognitive habit of recognizing the edges of one's own knowledge, keep finding the same surprise. A comprehensive review in Nature Reviews Psychology links intellectual humility to sharper judgment, better-calibrated beliefs, and reduced susceptibility to bias. Humility, in other words, operates as a precision instrument. It sharpens the very faculties that grandiosity dulls.

Hybrid humility places that mindset in a reality where artificial intelligence is increasingly all-pervasive. It invites us to ask: What belongs to me, and what am I borrowing from a machine, a title, an institution, an inherited certainty? The question scales up too. A species that has spent a century mistaking its tools for its character keeps rediscovering, generation after generation, that the tool was only ever the vehicle.

Carving the Self, Not Outsourcing It

The destination has nothing to do with becoming superhuman through sharper prosthetics, whether radioactive water, gene maps, or large language models. Every one of those episodes promised us an upgrade delivered from outside. Hybrid humility points the search inward: toward the self a person already carries, and toward the collective self a species already carries, both waiting to be drawn out with more honesty than either has managed so far. Individually, that means noticing which parts of a day are chosen and which parts run on autopilot borrowed from a screen. Collectively, it means building systems that amplify human judgment rather than replace the practice of forming it, then passing whatever best self surfaces on to whoever comes next.

The Friday Question

One practice makes this concrete without requiring a retreat, a course, or an app.

Ask yourself: if I died next Friday, what would I leave behind? Would I be proud of it?

The question sounds morbid until the research catches up with it. Humans who think seriously about the mark they will leave, according to researchers studying what they call legacy motivation, report greater meaning, higher life satisfaction, and stronger flourishing than people who never ask, with the strongest effects among those focused on genuine impact rather than on being remembered fondly. A separate strand of management research has turned the same instinct into a working method, showing that deliberately activating legacy motivation moves people toward more concrete, more generous decisions almost immediately.

Try the Friday question on an ordinary Tuesday. Notice what surfaces first: a project, a relationship, an apology undelivered, a talent left folded in a drawer somewhere. That inventory is the one a glowing bottle of radium water could never supply, and no chatbot can generate on your behalf.

Where the Path Actually Leads

Every generation gets convinced it has found the shortcut past its own limits. Every generation, in hindsight, finds it had located one more step on a walk that was always going to be long. Hybrid humility names the willingness to take that step without mistaking it for the destination, from the inside out, one honest Friday at a time.

item.title: "Why Won't You Initiate Sex More?"
item.description:
Sex

"Why Won't You Initiate Sex More?"

What's really going on when partners are in conflict about who initiates.

Posted August 8, 2026

Key points
  • If someone doesn't enjoy sex much, don't expect them to initiate it.
  • If a partner won't initiate sex much, don't assume it's a comment on how much you're loved.
  • When your partner won't initiate sex, don't create so much conflict about it that sex disappears altogether.
  • Whether or not people initiate sex often depends on nonsexual issues.

Every week or two, a new patient complains that their partner rarely initiates sex. The new patient expects me to figure out why—and more importantly, how to get their partner to change and initiate more.

People who rarely initiate sex fall into one of three categories:
a) They like the sex they have.
b) They like sex, but not the sex that’s available.
c) They don’t much care for sex.

Do You Like Asparagus?

If someone doesn’t care for sex, expecting them to initiate it is unrealistic (I don’t like asparagus, and no one is surprised that I don’t cook it or order it in restaurants). That couple needs a different conversation, perhaps about whether to continue the relationship.

If someone likes sex but doesn’t like the sex that’s available in their current relationship, expecting them to initiate it is also unrealistic. These couples need to figure out how to make the sex more appealing to both parties. This may involve sexual changes (less of this, more of that, an end to certain requests), or nonsexual changes (less drinking, less teasing, less bullying; less self-criticism, fewer fantasies about being judged; a redistribution of household chores or parenting routines or rules about finances).

So let’s talk about partners who like sex more or less as it is—except for the initiating part. These people often say things like:

  • “I’m always being criticized for my inadequate desire.”
  • “When I do initiate, she says I do it wrong.”
  • “He doesn’t even give me a chance to initiate; he’s always on top of me.”
  • “He complains all the time that we don’t have enough sex.”

Conditions like these are enough to discourage anyone from initiating sex.

In addition, people who don’t initiate sometimes have complicated emotions about it, such as “I feel clumsy when I initiate,” or “I was always told initiating sex wasn’t ladylike,” or “I’m afraid you’ll laugh at me or say no if I do suggest sex.”

Let's Look at It Differently

But let’s look at the inverse: Why do some people get so distressed when their partner doesn’t initiate?

Those people often say:

  • “I want to feel desired.”
  • “If I didn’t initiate, we’d never have sex.”
  • “I need to know she really wants sex.”
  • “We hardly ever have sex anymore.”
article continues after advertisement

Of course, if the complaint is “we hardly ever have sex,” the question isn’t, "Why won’t my partner initiate?" It’s "Why doesn’t my partner want sex with me?" Your partner has the answer and may disclose it if you ask directly—especially if it’s not in the middle of the same old late-night argument.

Unfortunately, some people have trouble feeling loved, or important, or attractive when their partner doesn’t initiate sex. Now it’s one thing to be disappointed if your partner doesn’t want sex as much as you do, or they don’t like to initiate. It’s entirely different to assign meaning to that, such as “if you don’t initiate, it means you don’t love me.”

Since most of us want to feel loved, it’s important that we each have multiple ways of getting and enjoying that feeling. These might include our partner doing favors for us (like one of our chores), or being affectionate, or doing activities we really like that they don’t, or supporting us in a difficult project, such as losing weight or quitting smoking.

I don’t like the simplistic “love languages” scheme, but it can help a couple who are stuck. In reality, your partner might be expressing love or attraction using a nonsexual (or non-initiating) vocabulary. Rather than complain that you can’t feel loved if your partner doesn’t initiate, you’re better off exploring, discussing, and learning alternative ways that you can feel loved.

Skiing? Sushi?

Couples generally don’t expect that they’ll desire their common interests exactly the same amount: You both ski, but one of you suggests it more often than the other. You both love sushi, but one of you suggests it more often. And no one complains, “Why don’t you suggest skiing or sushi more often?”

But somehow with sex, many people expect that two people’s appetites or styles will be exactly the same. And that’s a rarity, whether a couple has a lot of sex or very little.

Enjoying being in a couple requires that we learn how to tolerate occasionally not getting what we want. Tolerating disappointment about one thing while you’re getting other things you do want is an important life skill. Put another way, anyone who wants to enjoy life will not let their disappointment about what they miss ruin their appreciation of what they have.

article continues after advertisement

When people are happy with the frequency and quality of their sex lives, they generally pay very little attention to who initiates. If you’re unhappy about either one, don’t waste time talking about who initiates; work together to figure out where your sexual interests/preferences overlap, identify how each of you wants to feel in the relationship, and talk about how you can arrange for that—regardless of your current sex life.
